allowed_titles: Monsieur (French address, period-authentic for Cajun Louisiana)
pun_style: Cajun-inflected bayou wordplay embedded in a surname or nickname — one witness gets a French-flavored name meaning 'saw everything' or similar; one gets a confection-trade pun. Keep subtle and pronounceable.
notes: November 1931 Depression-era Louisiana: Cajun and Creole naming conventions dominate. Surnames are French or French-corrupted (Delacroix, Fontenot, Tureaud, Arcand). Given names lean heavily Catholic-saint or French-provincial. Traveling mud-show circus slang of the era: 'lot' for grounds, 'bull-hand' for elephant keeper, 'talker' not 'barker' (barker was considered an insult in the trade), 'fil-de-fer' for wire-walker (French circus term), 'roustabout' for general labor. Honorific 'Doc' is permissible only in casual spoken dialogue, never formal address. The Great Depression context means the circus is struggling financially — relevant to character motivations. Flood-season bayou setting adds isolation; the town is semi-submerged, so the circus lot is on elevated shell road or levee ground.
